To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the eye is not drawn to image discontinuities but rather to places in the visual field that have been selected for inspection by a task-based process that determines the sequence in which visual information will be gathered from the scene.

(i) the eye is drawn towards places in the visual field that contain the features that will enable a task to be accomplished; (ii) the features of the visual scene that attract the eye are the same features that are used by the brain to construct a representation of the scene; and (iii) the eye is not drawn to places that contain features that are not relevant to any task that the observer is engaged in.
(a) the eye is drawn towards the target of a visual task; (b) the target is defined by the task and not by image properties; and (c) the target is selected by a process of visual search.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the role of task and its interaction with the environment in determining eye movements.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

(a) the eye moves to acquire information that is relevant to the task; (b) the task determines the information required and the way in which it must be acquired; (c) the eye moves in a manner that optimizes the acquisition of the task-relevant information; (d) the eye does not move to acquire image features, except in so far as they happen to be relevant to the task

fixations are controlled by a task-based system, and that the visual system is tuned so that it responds to the presence of image discontinuities, which are the consequence of the task-based control of fixation.
fixations are controlled by the task being performed and are directed to locations in the scene that will provide information that is relevant to that task.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the visual system is not concerned with the image features themselves, but only with the information they carry about the world.
the eye is controlled by the task, and the eye is the task.
task is the dominant influence on fixation control, but that image features are also important, and that the influence of task and image features are not necessarily mutually exclusive.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the control of fixation is not an end in itself, but a means to a visual end.
, in general, fixation control is driven by a task that the observer is trying to accomplish, and that the image features that attract attention are a consequence rather than the cause of fixation.
the visual system does not just respond to image-based events in the environment, but actively searches for them in order to serve some task.
